h1: California HOA Lien & Foreclosure Threat Response Letter Generator
metaTitle: California HOA Lien Foreclosure Demand Letter Tool
metaDescription: Generate a California HOA lien or foreclosure threat response demand letter. Cite Davis-Stirling Act protections, dispute charges, and stop wrongful foreclosure.
statuteCitation: California Civil Code §§ 5650-5740 (Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act)
deadline: 90 days before recording a lien; 30 days to request dispute resolution after pre-lien notice
penalty: A lien recorded without the required notice or board vote can be challenged; delinquent assessments under $1,800 (excluding late charges, fees, costs, attorney's fees, and interest) cannot be collected by foreclosure unless they are more than 12 months delinquent (Civ. Code § 5720)
introParagraph: If your California HOA has threatened to record a lien on your home or pursue nonjudicial foreclosure over unpaid assessments, you have powerful rights under the Davis-Stirling Act. California gives homeowners some of the strongest HOA foreclosure protections in the country, including a $1,800 minimum debt threshold, mandatory pre-lien notice, the right to a payment plan, and the right to internal dispute resolution (IDR) or alternative dispute resolution (ADR) before any foreclosure can proceed. A well-drafted response letter that cites the correct Civil Code sections often stops collection abuse, forces the HOA to itemize charges, and prevents an improperly recorded lien from ripening into a forced sale of your home.
lawExplanation: California HOA assessment collection is governed by the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act, codified at Civil Code §§ 4000-6150, with the lien and foreclosure rules concentrated in §§ 5650-5740. Before an HOA can record a lien, Civil Code § 5660 requires the association to mail the homeowner, by certified mail, a pre-lien notice at least 30 days in advance. That notice must itemize the assessments, late charges, interest, and collection costs; describe the homeowner's right to inspect association records; explain the right to request a meeting with the board to discuss a payment plan under § 5665; and explain the right to dispute the debt through the association's dispute resolution process (§§ 5900-5920) and to request ADR (§§ 5925-5965) before the association may initiate foreclosure. If the HOA fails to satisfy any of these prerequisites, the lien is invalid and unenforceable. Even after a lien is properly recorded, Civil Code § 5720 strictly limits foreclosure: the HOA cannot use judicial or nonjudicial foreclosure if the delinquent assessments (excluding accelerated assessments, late fees, attorneys' fees, and interest) are less than $1,800, unless they are more than 12 months delinquent. The decision to foreclose must be made by the board in an executive session by a recorded vote, and the homeowner must be offered the chance to meet with the board. Civil Code § 5673 requires that the recording of a lien be approved by the board in an open meeting by majority vote. Civil Code § 5655 mandates that any payments made by a homeowner be applied first to assessments owed, before late fees, interest, or collection costs—a rule HOAs and their collection agents frequently violate. Violations of these statutes can void the lien and expose the HOA to damages and attorneys' fees.
letterStrategy: An effective California HOA lien response letter does several things at once. First, it formally disputes the debt; under Civil Code § 5658, where the amount in dispute is within the small claims limit the owner may pay the disputed amount under protest and sue in small claims court, in addition to pursuing dispute resolution. Second, it demands a complete itemized accounting separating principal assessments from late fees, interest, attorneys' fees, and collection costs, and challenges any misapplication of payments under § 5655. Third, it invokes the homeowner's statutory right to request a meeting with the board on a payment plan under § 5665, to use the association's dispute resolution procedure (§§ 5900-5910), and to request ADR (§§ 5925-5965) before the association may initiate foreclosure (§ 5660). Fourth, where the HOA failed to send a compliant pre-lien notice under § 5660 or failed to approve the lien by board vote under § 5673, the letter puts the association on written notice of those defects and demands release of the lien. Finally, the letter cites § 5720's $1,800 and 12-month thresholds to make clear that foreclosure is not legally available for a smaller, newer delinquency, and warns that wrongful recording or foreclosure may lead to claims such as slander of title and wrongful foreclosure, with attorney's fees where a statute or the governing documents allow them. A clear, statute-specific letter sent by certified mail frequently causes management companies and HOA collection law firms to halt foreclosure, correct accounting errors, and negotiate reasonable payment terms rather than litigate.
proceduralNotes: California's small claims limit for individuals is $12,500, which can be useful for recovering overcharges, improperly applied payments, or damages from a wrongful lien. However, claims to quiet title, void a lien, or stop foreclosure must be filed in superior court—small claims cannot grant injunctive relief. Filing fees in superior court range from approximately $225 to $450 depending on the amount in controversy, with fee waivers available for low-income homeowners. The statute of limitations for breach of the CC&Rs is generally five years (Code of Civil Procedure § 336(b)). Homeowners facing imminent foreclosure should consider filing for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction. Civil Code § 5975(c) entitles the prevailing party in an action to enforce the governing documents to reasonable attorneys' fees.

faq.q: Can my California HOA foreclose on my home for a small unpaid assessment?
faq.a: No. Under Civil Code § 5720, a California HOA cannot use judicial or nonjudicial foreclosure if the delinquent regular or special assessments are less than $1,800, unless they are more than 12 months delinquent. Late fees, interest, attorneys' fees, and collection costs do not count toward the $1,800 threshold. If your unpaid assessments fall below both limits, the HOA can still record a lien and sue you in court, but it cannot force a trustee's sale of your home. Many HOA threats violate this rule.

faq.q: What must the HOA do before recording a lien on my property?
faq.a: Under Civil Code § 5660, the HOA must mail you a pre-lien notice by certified mail at least 30 days before recording. The notice must itemize all charges, describe your right to inspect association records, explain your right to request a meeting with the board on a payment plan (§ 5665), and notify you of your right to dispute resolution (§§ 5900-5920) and ADR (§§ 5925-5965). The board must also vote to approve the lien by majority vote of the directors in an open meeting under § 5673, and the vote must be recorded in the minutes.

faq.q: Does the HOA have to accept a payment plan?
faq.a: Civil Code § 5665 lets an owner submit a written request to meet with the board to discuss a payment plan, and the association must provide the standards for payment plans, if any exist. The board must meet with the owner in executive session within 45 days of the postmark of the request if the request is mailed within 15 days of the postmark of the notice, and additional late fees do not accrue while the owner complies with the plan. Many associations have written payment plan policies. Refusing to engage in any discussion can be evidence of bad faith and may support claims if the HOA later forecloses without exhausting collection alternatives.

faq.q: How are my payments applied if I owe assessments and late fees?
faq.a: Civil Code § 5655(a) requires that any payment you make be applied FIRST to the assessments owed, and only after assessments are fully paid can the HOA apply funds to fees, collection costs, attorneys' fees, late charges, or interest. This is a critical protection because it prevents the HOA from keeping your account perpetually delinquent by skimming payments off to fees first. If your HOA or its collection agency has misapplied payments, you can demand correction and dispute the resulting lien or foreclosure threat.

faq.q: What happens if the HOA records a lien improperly?
faq.a: An improperly recorded lien is void and unenforceable. You can demand the HOA record a release of the lien, and if it refuses, you may sue to quiet title and for slander of title. Under Civil Code § 5975(c), the prevailing party in an action to enforce the governing documents is entitled to reasonable attorneys' fees, which often makes attorney representation feasible. A clear demand letter citing the specific statutory violations frequently prompts the HOA's counsel to release the lien rather than risk fee-shifting litigation.
